blocks.heading: AIDA as an advertising guide
blocks.text: AIDA is a simple way of planning an advert’s design: attention, interest, desire and action. Attract attention so the target notices; build interest with a relevant message; develop desire by connecting a credible benefit to need; make the next action clear. It is a planning guide, not a guarantee that every viewer moves through a fixed sequence or buys. Keep it distinct from the marketing mix of product, price, promotion and place or distribution. AIDA helps shape a promotional message within that wider mix.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nela Bags uses a clear headline, shows tool compartments, explains easier organisation and gives the collection point and opening time. These respectively support attention, interest, desire and action. A bright headline without relevant information or a buying route is an incomplete advert.

blocks.heading: Attention in AIDA
blocks.text: Attention means getting the target audience to notice the advert. A clear relevant headline or image can help it stand out, but excessive clutter can hide the message. Attention is a starting requirement, not evidence that a person wants or buys the product.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Omi Bags uses a clear tool-storage headline. It can attract the intended buyer’s attention more usefully than an unrelated bright image.

blocks.heading: Interest in AIDA
blocks.text: Interest means engaging the viewer with relevant information after attracting attention. Show what the offering does and why it relates to the target’s needs. An attention-grabbing claim without useful detail can lose the audience before it understands the benefit.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Omi Bags shows labelled compartments and capacity. The detail helps a prospective tradesperson see whether the bag is relevant.

blocks.heading: Desire in AIDA
blocks.text: Desire means developing a wish for the offering by connecting credible benefits with the customer’s needs. It goes beyond noticing features to seeing their value. It must not assume all viewers share the same priorities or replace evidence with an unsupported promise.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Omi Bags explains easier access to organised tools. The benefit can create preference if customers value it and the design delivers it.

blocks.heading: Action in AIDA
blocks.text: Action means making the intended next step clear, such as how to order, visit, enquire or buy. Supply accessible contact or collection information and relevant timing. A customer who wants the product may still fail to act if no practical route is shown.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Omi Bags gives its workshop collection point and stated opening hours. The information helps interested customers take the next step rather than merely remember the name.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why product, price, promotion and distribution are not the four letters of AIDA. A fictional advert uses a headline, useful detail, a credible benefit and a clear ordering route.

AIDA means attention, interest, desire and action, describing how the advert is designed to encourage a response. Product, price, promotion and distribution are the wider marketing-mix decisions. The advert is part of promotion within that mix.
